---
title: "Python answer tests"
subtitle: "Basis questions, matrix conditions and your own checker"
---

A question may have many mathematically correct answers. This guide helps you
choose a test for a space or property and shows how ordinary STACK response
trees (PRTs) continue to award the marks. The [worked questions](../examples.qmd)
let you try each choice.

## For teachers

### Choose the mathematical test {#choose-the-mathematical-test}

| Task | Test | What counts as correct |
|---|---|---|
| Give this particular matrix | `AlgEquiv` | Corresponding entries are equivalent and dimensions agree. |
| Give any basis of a matrix's null, column or row space | `IsBasis` | Independent vectors span that space, regardless of the particular basis chosen. |
| Give any basis of a space specified by basis vectors | `IsBasis` | Independent vectors have the same span as the reference vectors. |
| Give a matrix satisfying the built-in conditions | `MatrixProperty` | Integer entries, a stated determinant or identity status. |
| Give a matrix satisfying another condition | `PythonChecker` | A named author function checks the stated property, such as positive definiteness. |

`AlgEquiv` is an existing STACK answer-test name. `IsBasis`, `MatrixProperty`
and `PythonChecker` are Python additions to this port. They keep STACK-style
inputs and PRT scoring, but a native Moodle STACK question needs equivalent
Maxima tests and may need different matrix-input settings.

### Basis questions: use the matrix in the question {#basis-questions-use-the-matrix-in-the-question}

If the prompt asks for a basis of $\ker A$, the PRT compares the learner's
proposed vectors against the **original matrix $A$**, not against one
precomputed list of basis vectors. Choose `nullspace`; use `columnspace` or
`rowspace` for the other two spaces. The input's model answer can be generated
from $A$ with the matching author helper. Another independent basis is still
correct. For example, if
$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix}$, both the columns of
$\begin{pmatrix}-2&-3\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and those of
$\begin{pmatrix}-5&-1\\1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ span $\ker A$.

| `IsBasis` option | Space being checked | How learners enter vectors |
|---|---|---|
| `nullspace` | Null space of the original $A$ | One vector per column |
| `columnspace` | Column space of the original $A$ | One vector per column |
| `rowspace` | Row space of the original $A$ | One vector per row |
| `columns` (default) | Span of independent reference columns supplied by the author | One vector per column |
| `rows` | Span of independent reference rows supplied by the author | One vector per row |

The older `columns` and `rows` modes answer a different question: they compare
spans with a supplied reference basis. Use them when that basis really defines
the space in the prompt. For a matrix-defined space, use the original-matrix
options above. The [basis examples](../examples.qmd#matrix-problems-from-ingmat-3a)
show alternate correct responses and learner-selected column counts. The
matrix editor cannot represent an empty basis, so choose a task with a
nonzero-dimensional answer space.

After checking a basis, green marks a nonzero vector in the target space when
the valid submitted vectors are independent; it can still belong to an
incomplete family. Yellow marks a dependent valid family and red marks zero
or out-of-space vectors. These colors explain the answer; the PRT awards marks
only for the complete basis in the examples. Edits and resizing clear the
colors.

### Matrix conditions and partial credit {#matrix-conditions-and-partial-credit}

The [determinant-one task](../examples.qmd#find-a-nonidentity-matrix-with-determinant-one)
accepts any integer $2\times2$ matrix with determinant $1$ except the
identity. Three PRTs give one third of the score each: integer entries,
determinant and nonidentity. An entry-by-entry comparison with the model
would reject other correct matrices.

| `MatrixProperty` option | Expected result supplied in PRT `tans` | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `integer_entries` | `true` or `false` | Are all entries integers? |
| `determinant` | An exact rational value such as `1` | Does this square matrix have that determinant? |
| `identity` | `true` or `false` | Is it the identity matrix? |

The PRT's `tans` is the **expected property result**, not the matrix in the
prompt. For determinant one it is `1`; for nonidentity it is `false`.
`MatrixProperty` covers these three conditions only. A different condition
calls for `PythonChecker` or an equivalent native STACK author calculation.

### Positive definite matrices {#symmetric-positive-definite-matrices}

The two activities distinguish a matrix's **structure** from its
**positivity**. For real matrices, the structural condition is symmetry
$A=A^T$. For complex matrices it is Hermitian symmetry $A=A^*$, where
$A^*=\overline A^{\,T}$ conjugates the entries as well as transposing.
These are one condition on different number domains: $A^*=A^T$ for real
entries.

The independent positivity test asks whether
$\operatorname{Re}(z^*Az)>0$ for every nonzero complex vector $z$. It can
hold even for a non-Hermitian matrix. Let $H=(A+A^*)/2$. Then
$\operatorname{Re}(z^*Az)=z^*Hz$, so Sylvester's criterion tests positivity
exactly by requiring every leading principal determinant of $H$ to be
positive. In the real case, this is $x^TAx>0$ and $H=(A+A^T)/2$. For
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ with real entries, the test is
$a>0$ and $ad-((b+c)/2)^2>0$, while symmetry separately requires $b=c$.

The first activity requires **both** properties, the usual positive
definite condition for a Hermitian matrix (symmetric in the real case).
The second gives half the marks for each independently. Four real
$2\times2$ examples show why the scoring choice matters:

| Matrix | Hermitian (symmetric here)? | Positive definite? | Combined / separate marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ | Yes | Yes | $1$ / $1$ |
| $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ | No | Yes | $0$ / $1/2$ |
| $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ | Yes | No | $0$ / $1/2$ |
| $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ | No | No | $0$ / $0$ |

Both activities accept integers and exact fractions in the real **and
imaginary** parts; enter `%i` for $i$. Try
`matrix([2,%i],[-%i,2])`: it is Hermitian and positive definite, with
leading determinants $2$ and $3$. By contrast,
`matrix([1,%i],[%i,1])` is not Hermitian but does satisfy the independent
positivity test because its Hermitian part is the identity. This is why
checking $A^T=A$ would give the wrong answer for complex entries.

Both activities use the same author Python file. The first uses the
combined `is_hpd` function for one true/false decision; its single PRT
awards full credit only when both conditions hold. Try the identity, the
complex example above, and a matrix that has only one property. The
[authoring walkthrough](#author-the-spd-checker) shows the file, XML and
Quarto block.

```{.stack-question #docs-spd-matrix}
#| file: ../questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml
#| question: A positive definite matrix
#| python-checkers: ../questions/spd-checker.py
#| review: true
```

[Download the question XML](../questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml) ·
[View the checker file](../questions/spd-checker.py) ·
[Try it with the other matrix examples](../examples.qmd#symmetric-positive-definite-matrix)

The second activity checks **Hermitian symmetry and positivity separately**.
It uses `is_hermitian` and `is_positive_definite` in two PRTs, each worth
half the total. A non-Hermitian matrix that passes positivity earns only
the positivity half; a Hermitian indefinite matrix earns only the symmetry
half. Separate PRTs are useful when each condition should have its own
marks and feedback. For an all-or-nothing task, use the combined checker
or gate the positivity test behind a successful symmetry branch.

```{.stack-question #docs-spd-separate}
#| file: ../questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml
#| question: Hermitian symmetry and positive definiteness separately
#| python-checkers: ../questions/spd-checker.py
#| review: true
```

[Download the two-PRT question XML](../questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml) ·
[Compare the two authoring patterns](#author-the-spd-checker)

## For developers

### Built-in matrix test XML

For a question about the null space of a matrix stored in author variable
`A`, make the input model answer `<tans>nullspace_basis(A)</tans>` and use
this PRT node:

```xml
<answertest>IsBasis</answertest>
<sans>ans</sans>
<tans>A</tans>
<testoptions>nullspace</testoptions>
```

Use `columnspace_basis(A)`/`columnspace` or `rowspace_basis(A)`/`rowspace`
for the corresponding tasks. The older `columns` and `rows` options instead
require a nonempty independent reference basis in PRT `tans`. If that basis
spans the wrong space, the test will grade the wrong target. The input model
is checked against the PRT at build time. Add qtests with another correct
basis, an incomplete or dependent family, and a vector outside the space.

The built-in Python matrix tests accept exact rational entries (integers and
fractions), not decimals or symbolic parameters. Matrix inputs have 1–16
rows or columns and at most 64 entries. Set enough learner-selectable columns
or rows for the answer; [matrix input](matrix-input.qmd) explains resizing.

For `MatrixProperty`, set `sans` to the matrix input and choose one of its three
options in `testoptions`. For determinant $1$, use `<tans>1</tans>` and
`<testoptions>determinant</testoptions>`; the input's own `tans` holds a model
matrix. Assign true/false branch scores on each PRT explicitly. The editor
never supplies cell marks.

### Author the positive-definiteness checker {#author-the-spd-checker}

Save this complete file as [`questions/spd-checker.py`](../questions/spd-checker.py).
It registers three functions. `is_hermitian` and `is_positive_definite`
are independent tests; `is_hpd` combines them. The same exact test handles
real and complex entries. Positivity is decided from the leading principal
determinants of the Hermitian part, including for a non-Hermitian submission:

```python
"""Check Hermitian symmetry and positivity for exact real or complex matrices."""


def hermitian(A):
    return A.rows == A.cols and A == A.H


def positive_definite(A):
    if A.rows != A.cols:
        return False
    # Re(z.H*A*z) equals z.H*H*z for real or complex matrices.
    H = (A + A.H) / 2
    return all(H[:k, :k].det() > 0 for k in range(1, H.rows + 1))


def check_property(ansm, expected, property_test, explanation):
    if any(part.is_Rational is not True
           for entry in ansm for part in entry.as_real_imag()):
        return {"valid": False, "correct": False,
                "feedback": "Use integers or exact fractions for the real and imaginary parts."}
    correct = bool(property_test(ansm)) == bool(expected)
    return {"valid": True, "correct": correct,
            "feedback": "" if correct else explanation}


def is_hermitian(ansm, expected):
    return check_property(ansm, expected, hermitian,
                          "The Hermitian-symmetry condition does not match the expected result.")


def is_positive_definite(ansm, expected):
    return check_property(ansm, expected, positive_definite,
                          "The positive-definiteness condition does not match the expected result.")


def is_hpd(ansm, expected):
    return check_property(ansm, expected,
                          lambda A: hermitian(A) and positive_definite(A),
                          "The Hermitian-positive-definiteness condition does not match the expected result.")


CHECKERS = {"is_hermitian": is_hermitian,
            "is_positive_definite": is_positive_definite,
            "is_hpd": is_hpd}
```

Each registered function receives the parsed learner matrix as `ansm` and
the PRT's expected property result as `expected`. This example checker
requires exact Gaussian-rational entries: both real and imaginary parts
must be integers or fractions, for example `1/2+%i/3`. The example XML
forbids decimal notation; the checker rejects symbolic or irrational
real or imaginary parts such as `sqrt(2)`. These are choices for this
example, not restrictions on all matrix inputs or custom checkers. A
well-formed matrix that fails the selected property follows its PRT's false
branch. A plain Python `True` or `False` can replace the dictionary when no
extra feedback is needed.

The [complete XML question](../questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml)
sets the matrix input's model answer to `<tans>matrix([1,0],[0,1])</tans>`,
which fixes the editor at $2\times2$ but does not limit correct responses to
the identity. Its PRT passes the expected property result and awards marks:

```xml
<answertest>PythonChecker</answertest>
<sans>ansm</sans>
<tans>true</tans>
<testoptions>is_hpd</testoptions>
<truescoremode>=</truescoremode><truescore>1</truescore>
<falsescoremode>=</falsescoremode><falsescore>0</falsescore>
```

The authored tests include real and complex entries, alternate positive
definite matrices, all four symmetry/positivity combinations, and negative
or singular cases. The checker decides whether the answer satisfies the
rule; the PRT branches own credit.

For separate marks, the [second XML question](../questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml)
uses the **same** matrix input and Python file. It has two response trees:

| PRT name | `testoptions` | `tans` | Weight | What it awards |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `symmetry` | `is_hermitian` | `true` | $0.5$ | Half the total when $A=A^*$ |
| `positivity` | `is_positive_definite` | `true` | $0.5$ | Half the total when $\operatorname{Re}(z^*Az)>0$ for all nonzero complex $z$ |

Each node's true branch has score `1` within its own half-weighted PRT; its
false branch has score `0`. The positive-definiteness check is **not** gated
on Hermitian symmetry, so a non-Hermitian matrix with a positive Hermitian
part earns half credit. The question gives separate success messages and
checker diagnostics for the two conditions. For an all-or-nothing PRT
without `is_hpd`, route the Hermitian-symmetry node's true branch to a
positive-definiteness node. Both
false branches score zero; only the second true branch scores one. That PRT
design and the Python wrapper enforce the same combined requirement, with
different places to manage the branch feedback.

Add either XML file and **only the checker filename** to a root-level Quarto page:

````markdown
```{.stack-question}
#| file: questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml
#| question: A positive definite matrix
#| python-checkers: questions/spd-checker.py
#| review: true
```
````

To use the separately weighted question, change `file` to
`questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml` and `question` to
`Hermitian symmetry and positive definiteness separately`; keep the same
checker file.
For a `.qmd` in `docs/`, use `../questions/...` instead. Quarto reads that
Python file at build time and includes its source for browser grading. The
XML names `is_hpd` but contains no Python code or file path. There is no
additional source configuration.

From the project root, test the authored cases and render:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=_extensions/stack-sympy python -m stack_sympy.cli test \
  --file questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml \
  --python-checkers questions/spd-checker.py
PYTHONPATH=_extensions/stack-sympy python -m stack_sympy.cli test \
  --file questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml \
  --python-checkers questions/spd-checker.py
quarto render
```

Inspect the live card and try an alternate correct answer such as
`matrix([2,%i],[-%i,2])` as well as a Hermitian matrix with nonpositive
determinant. Try `matrix([1,%i],[%i,1])` in the separate task to see
positivity earn half credit without Hermitian symmetry. Both scoring choices
have [teaching cards](#symmetric-positive-definite-matrices)
and [examples-page cards](../examples.qmd#symmetric-positive-definite-matrix).

### PythonChecker API and a scalar example


Use `PythonChecker` when the built-in tests do not express the condition. Save
a Python file beside your question materials, register a named function in
its `CHECKERS` dictionary, then give Quarto that **filename** in
`#| python-checkers:`. Quarto reads the file when it builds the page and
includes its source for browser grading; the XML only names the function.
The [positive-multiple example](../examples.qmd#custom-python-checker) checks any
positive integer multiple of a given number. Its author module contains:

```python
def positive_multiple(student, teacher):
    if student.is_Integer is not True:
        return {"valid": False, "correct": False,
                "feedback": "Enter an integer value."}
    return bool(student > 0 and student % teacher == 0)

CHECKERS = {"positive_multiple": positive_multiple}
```

The XML names the checker and passes the learner input and teacher value:

```xml
<answertest>PythonChecker</answertest>
<sans>ans</sans>
<tans>d</tans>
<testoptions>positive_multiple</testoptions>
```

Select the module on the Quarto question block as well:

```{.stack-question #docs-custom-multiple}
#| file: ../questions/python-checker.xml
#| question: A positive integer multiple (PythonChecker)
#| python-checkers: ../questions/checkers.py
#| variants: 3
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

Both filenames in this block are relative to this `.qmd` page. For the CLI,
filenames are relative to the working directory. There is no separate source
configuration to maintain. `sans` must directly name
an input. `tans` can be a parsed teacher answer or author value, such as the
divisor `d`; `testoptions` names one entry in `CHECKERS`. It is a single
case-sensitive ASCII identifier of at most 64 characters, beginning with a letter
and followed by letters, digits, or underscores. It is not a file path or a
Python expression. The selected module is author code packaged with the page;
use only code you trust and expect learners to be able to see in a published
site.

#### Callable and values

Each registered function must be callable with the two positional arguments
`student` and `teacher`, and finish synchronously. They are parsed values, not
raw answer strings. The function receives the submitted answer and whatever
teacher value the PRT's `tans` selects. This could be an expected Boolean for
a property question or a reference matrix for a different task. The API does
not pass a context object, question state or separate configuration argument.
Scalar expressions are SymPy expressions; matrices are
immutable SymPy matrices. Lists and finite sets are distinct `ListValue` and
`SetValue` objects with ordered `.args` (a set retains its submitted entries).
Equations have two `.args`; held logic has `.operator` and `.operands`;
logical constants use SymPy `true` and `false`. The collection and logic types
and `collection_items` are available from `stack_sympy.checker_api`.
These values do not promise to retain the learner's exact written arithmetic
form. A custom checker decides its own mathematical domain, within the
existing input and parser limits.

Return a Python `bool` for an ordinary true/false decision, or a dictionary:

```python
{"valid": True, "correct": False, "feedback": "Try another value."}
```

Both required fields must be Python booleans. Use `valid=False` for a response
outside this checker's domain: the learner sees an invalid-input diagnostic
and the PRT's false branch does not run. Use `valid=True, correct=False` for
a mathematically wrong response within the domain. `feedback` is optional
plain text of at most 4,096 characters. A checker cannot return a score or an
answer note; the PRT branches control those. Exceptions and malformed results
are authoring errors, rather than wrong student answers.

For a matrix, a valid result may also include one diagnostic axis:

```python
{"valid": True, "correct": False,
 "assessment": {"columns": ["correct", "dependent"]}}
```

Choose exactly `rows` or `columns`, with one status per submitted vector.
Statuses are `correct`, `incorrect`, or `dependent`. They color the editor but
do not award marks. A checker may omit the assessment entirely. If several
visited PRT nodes supply an assessment for one input, the last one displayed
wins. A quiet PRT node suppresses its checker diagnostic and assessment. The result
cannot include extra keys, an assessment for an invalid response, or a
SymPy Boolean in place of a Python `bool`.

#### Test and publish

Run authored tests with the same module you render:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=_extensions/stack-sympy python -m stack_sympy.cli test \
  --file questions/python-checker.xml --python-checkers questions/checkers.py
```

The build checks referenced names, function signatures and model-answer
grading on each rendered variant. Add qtests for alternative correct answers, wrong
answers, and important PRT branches. **Validate answers** checks syntax and
input rules; the custom predicate runs on **Check answer**. The page includes
the selected Python source so the same checker runs in local tests and the
learner's browser. Keep secrets out of the module, use available Python and
SymPy features, and avoid local imports or services that the browser cannot
provide. Make checker functions deterministic; do not rely on module state
persisting from one check, variant or test to the next. Custom code can perform
arbitrary computation, so review it before
publishing. The API does not install packages or add new input types. For code
that imports questions directly, `import_xml(xml_path, python_checkers=module_path)`
selects the source; call `stack_sympy.checkers.preflight(question, variants)`
before publication to run the same author checks. `grade()` and
`run_question_tests()` execute the selected predicate on visited PRT nodes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Technical limits

A module may register at most 32 named functions in `CHECKERS`. Its source
must be a nonempty UTF-8 file no larger than 64 KiB. Feedback is plain text
up to 4,096 characters. Custom execution does not gain a server process or
additional package installation; apply a process timeout to local test runs
if authored code could take a long time.
:::
